the coiled-coil domain is not sufficient to confer IF recognition, and that IF recognition is a function of the entire molecule.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular basis for IF recognition and assembly and the consequences of IF network segregation on the structure and organization of the cell cytoplasm.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the coiled-coil domain of IF proteins is necessary but not sufficient for IF network recognition and assembly.
IF networks are not simply composed of 10-nm filaments but are also composed of higher ordered IF assemblies, which are regulated at the level of the IF protein itself.
the IF network is a complex system of interactions, with a variety of factors contributing to the formation of IFs and IF networks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
swapping of helices is not as disruptive as deletion, but it does affect filament structure and IF network interactions.
the IF network is a highly ordered, dynamic system in which the IF subunit composition and the organization of the IF network itself are intimately linked.

IF proteins are not just coiled coils but rather that they are a family of proteins with distinct structural and functional features that can be exploited by nature to generate a variety of IF networks.
The main takeaway from our work is that
IF recognition and assembly are not independent processes and that the two are intimately connected.
IF proteins have the ability to recognize each other and segregate into different IF networks in the absence of other IF-associated molecules.
the IF network in a cell is not a random assembly of IF proteins but rather a very organized and specific assembly of IF subunits.
